article_title: A movement and story-telling intervention improves language and fundamental movement skills and is feasible for delivery by teachers in the first year of school
citation: Cunningham, Anna J.; Baikousi, Violeta; Eyre, Emma; Duncan, Michael; Crotti, Matteo; Martins, Ricardo; Wood, Clare. (2025). A movement and story-telling intervention improves language and fundamental movement skills and is feasible for delivery by teachers in the first year of school. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://hdl.handle.net/10446/299265
title: Upskill early years educators and educate school management on the importance of teaching movement and language skills to young children
description: The article draws an implementation implication from its trial of MAST, a 12-week whole-class combined movement and story-telling approach delivered by teachers. Because the programme proved feasible but fidelity varied, the authors state that "Implications include the need to upskill early years educators and to educate school management on the importance of teaching movement and language skills to young children". This positions educator training and management buy-in as prerequisites for successfully delivering integrated movement and language programmes in school.
requirements: Teachers need upskilling to deliver combined movement and story-telling programmes as delivered in MAST
constraints: Fidelity varied: one of five schools did not consistently deliver all key components of MAST
target_learners: four-to-five-year-old children in the first year of primary school
examples: MAST, a 12-week whole-class combined movement and story-telling approach, was delivered by teachers across five primary schools in a cluster-randomised controlled trial with 214 children
key_sources: Cunningham, Anna J.; Baikousi, Violeta; Eyre, Emma; Duncan, Michael; Crotti, Matteo; Martins, Ricardo; Wood, Clare. (2025). A movement and story-telling intervention improves language and fundamental movement skills and is feasible for delivery by teachers in the first year of school. LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION. https://hdl.handle.net/10446/299265

article_title: The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers
citation: Bosch, N., & D'Mello, S. (2017). The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0069-5
title: Updated model of affect dynamics and co-occurrence during complex learning, adding a boredom→engagement re-engagement link and co-occurrence arcs
description: The article tests the D'Mello and Graesser affect dynamics model, in which engagement, confusion, frustration, and boredom interact through impasse detection and resolution, and proposes a revision based on its findings. The revised model (Fig. 7) keeps the impasse-driven cycle but, as the authors state, "Figure 7 presents an updated theoretical model incorporating the new affect transition as well as co-occurrences" — replacing the boredom→frustration link with a boredom→engagement re-engagement link and adding arcs for the confusion+frustration and curiosity+engagement co-occurrence pairs, plus a curiosity (novelty) state.
requirements: Applies to complex learning situations with impasses, tested here for novice computer programming with fine-grained (15-s interval) affect judgments
constraints: The predicted boredom→frustration transition was not significant in this data; the boredom→engagement transition, though observed, was attributed to the fast-paced, hint-supported nature of this particular learning environment
target_learners: novice computer programming students without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: learning fundamentals of computer programming in Python
examples: The study tested the original model against affect transition likelihoods from 99 novices and found five of six predicted transitions significant, motivating the revised model in Fig. 7
key_sources: Bosch, N., & D'Mello, S. (2017). The Affective Experience of Novice Computer Programmers. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0069-5

article_title: Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review.
citation: Iop A., El-Hajj V.G., Gharios M., de Giorgio A., Monetti F.M., Edström E., Elmi-Terander A., Romero M. (2022). Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22166067
title: UP/UX metric framework for evaluating XR educational simulations
description: The review defines user performance (UP) as "a set of metrics that quantifies the efficiency and effectiveness of a surgical simulation carried out on an XR system", including accuracy, precision, surgical outcome, speed, and attempts per user. User experience (UX) accounts for how subjects perceive events, interactions, and feedback, organized into ten categories: usefulness, self-assessment, haptic interaction, ease of use, system feedback, comfort, time requirements, engagement, immersiveness, and realism. The framework is used to group indicators across the 31 included studies and to detect which metrics are shared versus study-specific.
requirements: Metrics must be classifiable as objective UP measures or subjective UX measures to allow grouping across studies
constraints: The review found UP metrics vary by procedure and UX questionnaires were mostly custom, hindering cross-study comparison
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and surgical skill acquisition in cranial neurosurgery
examples: Tumor resection studies grouped UP metrics into three tiers: percentage of tumor resected and healthy tissue volume (tier 1), time and instrument path length (tier 2), and kinematic force metrics (tier 3)
key_sources: Iop A., El-Hajj V.G., Gharios M., de Giorgio A., Monetti F.M., Edström E., Elmi-Terander A., Romero M. (2022). Extended Reality in Neurosurgical Education: A Systematic Review. Sensors. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22166067

article_title: An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case-based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education.
citation: Lundegren N, Jönsson A, Lindberg P. (2021). An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case‐based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education. European Journal of Dental Education, 25(4), 649-656. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12642
title: The upgraded Malmö model: case-based teaching with flipped classroom seminars replacing pure PBL in dental education
description: The upgraded Malmö model retains the original model's pillars while replacing pure problem-based learning with case-based teaching, in which teachers design cases and provide direction, study materials and structure. The original model rested on activation of prior knowledge, encoding specificity by contextual learning and elaboration of knowledge, with pillars including "Active learning—actively engaging students through discussions, problem‐solving, case studies, roleplay and other methods." Cases are introduced gradually, and learning activities such as flipped classroom seminars, quizzes and peer-assessed assignments are added. The change responded to rising examination failure rates and students struggling with the responsibility PBL demands.
requirements: Teachers must design cases based on subject-matter expertise and provide thorough study instructions with clear learning goals and literature references
Students need some degree of prior knowledge to address the cases, unlike PBL
constraints: Not all knowledge and understanding objectives are studied through cases; teacher-directed delivery of disciplinary knowledge is used for some objectives
Group work is mandatory only during the first year, thereafter voluntary but highly encouraged
target_learners: undergraduate dental students (also dental technicians and dental hygienists in the original model)
examples: From the first semester in 2018, the faculty moved from PBL to case-based teaching, following Licari's three steps for curriculum change and using two early adopters as mentors
key_sources: Lundegren N, Jönsson A, Lindberg P. (2021). An upgrade of the Malmö model by implementing case‐based teaching and learning, in an undergraduate dental education. European Journal of Dental Education, 25(4), 649-656. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.12642

article_title: Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study.
citation: Sintayehu Y, Assefa D, Biftu G, Getahun T, Haymanot M, Kasiye S, Teshale M. (2020). Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0236194
title: Encourage providers to upgrade their educational level and gain practical exposure to neonatal resuscitation to build skill retention
description: The article recommends that health system planners and educators support midwives and nurses in raising their qualification level and gaining hands-on NR experience, because both were independently associated with skill retention. As the conclusion states, "Providers should be encouraged to upgrade their educational level to build their skill retention and expose themselves to NR." This links educational investment and clinical exposure to sustained resuscitation competence.
requirements: Providers must have access to degree-level education pathways and opportunities to perform NR in clinical practice
constraints: Based on a cross-sectional study at one time point, so cause-effect relationships could not be established
target_learners: In-service midwives and nurses in public health facilities in low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Retention of basic neonatal resuscitation skills
examples: In the study, 68.4% of participants held a BSc degree or above and 47.3% had ever performed NR; these characteristics predicted who retained skills
key_sources: Sintayehu Y, Assefa D, Biftu G, Getahun T, Haymanot M, Kasiye S, Teshale M. (2020). Basic neonatal resuscitation skills of midwives and nurses in Eastern Ethiopia are not well retained: An observational study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0236194
